#3239. Why Engineers Should Brave Capitol Hill

Congress needs accurate technical insights

Lucas Laursen is the technology policy editor at IEEE Spectrum.

During this year’s Congressional Visits Day, Nikhil Jathar [second from left] and three other IEEE members met with Nile Whitmore [middle], a legislative assistant for Representative Greg Casar (D-Texas).

When San Antonio–based software engineer Nikhil Jathar first went to Washington, D.C., to advocate for federal support for technology education and research funding, he was in awe of the opportunity. It was spring of 2025, not long after Jathar settled in the United States from India, when he got an invitation to join the annual Congressional Visits Day organized by IEEE-USA.

“My first reaction was, ‘Wow, I get to visit Congress,’ ” says Jathar, CTO of AvanSaber, a business software company he cofounded in 2014. At the time, he did not have a specific lobbying position on behalf of the company. But he was intrigued by the invitation—which goes out to all U.S. IEEE members—and as he read more about congressional visits, his motivation deepened. He realized: “I need to try this. I want to see where it goes.”

What’s Your Ask? Congressional staffers expect clarity from advocates. Be clear on what you plan to ask for when you arrive. Here are some common options:Cosponsor (or oppose) an existing bill or amendment.Preserve, remove, or modify legislative text in a bill under consideration.Add language to an appropriations bill or committee report.Ask a federal agency a specific oversight question.Request a briefing, hearing, Government Accountability Office review, or stakeholder roundtable.Encourage an agency to clarify a technical rule.

Congressional staffers expect clarity from advocates. Be clear on what you plan to ask for when you arrive. Here are some common options:

Congressional staffers say they welcome the knowledge and perspective that engineers like Jathar and other visitors from beyond Washington, D.C., provide. It’s also important for those visitors to be clear on what they are advocating for. One staffer for the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, who agreed to speak anonymously due to the office’s media policy, says, “Ideas for new policies come from multiple places. It could begin at the [legislator] or staff level, an ask from a constituent, or needs from industry. It’s up to us to figure out what would do the most good,” the staffer said. “For instance, if you leave it to the lobbyists, they’re understandably going to do what’s in their clients’ interests.”

For engineers in the United States, speaking with elected representatives is an effective way to shape key policies, but it takes some preparation and the right approach, as Jathar learned over the course of two visits.

Congress’s job is to act on behalf of the people, and it has rules for how people can lobby it. It distinguishes between broader advocacy—conversations between constituents and U.S. representatives—and professional lobbying, which involves paid professionals and is governed by the Lobbying Disclosure Act. Many professional groups like IEEE also organize congressional visits for their members. Those visits can be subject to lobbying rules, so the organizers told Jathar that: “You are representing the organization, not your own views.” He would need to stick to the talking points IEEE-USA had prepared for all its participants, regardless of their specialty, to promote across several congressional offices.

On Jathar’s first visit, those organizational talking points included advocating for funding smart grids, authorizing Department of Energy research, and investing in STEM education. That represents one of the trade-offs of access in Washington. IEEE-USA’s priorities didn’t all overlap directly with Jathar’s work, but they were broad enablers of science and technology and, he says, “STEM education funding is close to my heart.”

Anyone can approach their representatives in Washington with their personal priorities, Jathar notes, but given how pressed for time congressional staff are, they are more likely to prioritize a meeting that represents the views of as many of their constituents as possible. “I could have gone outside the IEEE structure,” Jathar says, but congressional staff “are more likely to listen if you are part of a much bigger organization.”

For Jathar’s first congressional visit, organizers assigned him to call on the offices of several representatives from both political parties based on where he lives: Representatives Greg Casar (D-Texas), Lloyd Doggett (D-Texas), and Barry Moore (R-Ala.). “Meeting a staffer or a senior member from their office is good. They tend to relate to these issues more than a representative, because a representative has 10 different high-level things they have to worry about whereas the staffer can be more focused on the policy details,” Jathar says.

A typical visit like this may last anywhere from 15 minutes to an hour, so Jathar kept his talking points simple and short. “First and foremost you’re gonna get a very small window,” he says, “Make sure you’ve got everything ready to present in bullet points and not a lot of jargon. You can always bring that out later if they ask more questions.” Simple visual aids, in the form of one-page handouts, may be helpful for communicating numeric or technical information, too.

“If you leave it to the lobbyists, they’re understandably going to do what’s in their clients’ interests.”–Staffer for the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology

The House Science Committee staffer agrees: “I prefer meetings where people know what they want and know what we’re doing in Congress.” In addition to having a clear request, the staffer says engineers and other advocates should keep track of where Congress is in its cycle: Is it appropriations season, and when is the next budget being set? How far along is a given piece of legislation in the process, and what is realistic to change at that point?

During Jathar’s 2025 visit to one Capitol Hill office, he learned firsthand the importance of preparation. For one of the three representatives he visited, staff politely pointed out that the legislator they worked for was not on the committee with jurisdiction over the IEEE-USA talking point they were discussing. “They explained that there are only certain things [the legislator] can do on that issue and that there are other people we need to talk to, to achieve more,” Jathar recalls.

Earlier this year, Jathar decided to go back to Capitol Hill with his newfound knowledge, again within the framework of an IEEE-USA visit. This time he was able to provide something else legislative staff want from engineers: authoritative technical knowledge.

“When I introduced myself as a software developer to one staffer, his first question was, ‘Do you think AI will replace coders?’ ” Jathar says. The conversation went back and forth, with the staffer asking Jathar and his other engineering companions questions. Jathar went on to explain that his company developed an open-source business-management software it calls ERPClaw, designed to be used with AI agents such as OpenClaw. That led naturally to discussing the role of open source in AI, which plays a role in one of IEEE-USA’s proposals for democratizing AI. This time Jathar was able to align his organization’s advocacy with his expertise and the staffer’s areas of interest.

It’s too soon to know what legislative impact that advocacy might have, but it’s the sort of informed, relevant proposal that legislative staff seek out. “The people who build trust have more cachet with congressional staff because they’ve asked for something that’s reasonably thought out,” the House Science Committee staffer says. In turn, congressional staffers can advocate better within their offices for policies brought to them by people they trust.

And talking about the issues you care the most about can deepen that trust. The House Science Committee staffer once visited Congress as an advocate before switching to the other side of the table. On that visit, as on Jathar’s, the professional society organizing the visit provided a pitch. “I was making a pitch that was given to me without a lot of personal buy-in,” the staffer says. Instead, “you should feel emotionally connected to any issue you’re advocating for.”

Jathar’s support for the open-source movement is like that. Open source gives smaller companies a foundation they can adapt and build upon, while allowing other developers to extend that work. “We can progress a lot faster,” Jathar says. “I’m not doing it only because it’s good for my business, but because I feel it’s good for any technological advancement.”

Lucas Laursen is the technology policy editor at IEEE Spectrum. He covers how emerging technologies are changing the balance of power between companies, governments, and individuals. The rest of the time, he worries about his own balance on a bicycle, skis, or the side of a mountain.

I found it difficult to get answers from legislative offices, so I'd love to hear what's missing in this story from any legislative staffers either here in the comments or at my email address (on our About page). I also know that things work somewhat differently in each country--are there readers in India or Germany or Chile who might be able to share their experiences working with lawmakers there?

#3236. Apple explains how to turn off the new MacBook Pro’s glowing logo

While the illuminated Apple logo on the new MacBook Pro drew one of the biggest cheers during last week’s announcement, Apple knows that not everyone will want to keep it on. Here’s the company’s official guide to turning it off.

The new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display marks the return of the illuminated Apple logo on its lid after a decade.

As Chance Miller explained in his review of the new MacBook Pro, “unlike older MacBooks, which used light from the display’s backlight to illuminate the logo, the new OLED MacBook Pro has no backlight to draw from, requiring a different approach.”

He added that, as with the old Macs, the logo’s brightness is tied to the screen brightness, though it also accounts for overall ambient brightness. He also noted that “when the MacBook Pro is closed, the logo looks like polished metal, just like it has since the 2016 redesign.”

The review echoed some of the findings developer Gui Rambo shared on X a few days ago:

The glowing Apple logo on the new MacBook Pro is controllable by software. It has 25kHz PWM and per-device calibration. CoreBrightness controls the relationship between screen and logo brightness. The brightness of the logo is adjusted differently depending on the enclosure color pic.twitter.com/baqBEkzJUo

Now, Apple has published an official support document that also explains how the illuminated logo works and how to turn it off completely.

The Apple logo behind the built-in display is illuminated whenever the Mac is awake. It automatically dims or brightens based on the brightness level of the built-in screen and the lighting conditions detected by the computer’s ambient light sensor. For all screen-brightness levels, the Apple logo will be dimmer in a dim room and brighter in a bright room.

For users who’d rather keep the logo turned off at all times, Apple explains that they can run the following command in Terminal, provided they have the administrator password:

sudo defaults write com.apple.CoreBrightness LEBacklightMode -int 0

Since it's actually two, opposite, single line command states;

Why can't it simply be an on/off button, in Settings?

To revert the command and have the logo be illuminated again, users will need to run the following command:

sudo defaults delete com.apple.CoreBrightness LEBacklightMode

Apple notes that reinstalling macOS will also turn the logo illumination back on.

#3235. Why AI Can’t Replace Engineering Teams

How to convince your boss LLMs can’t do it all

Brian Jenney is the owner of Parsity, a program that helps engineers through hands-on training.

This article is crossposted from IEEE Spectrum’s careers newsletter. Sign up now to get insider tips, expert advice, and practical strategies, written in partnership with tech career development company Parsity and delivered to your inbox for free!

If you’re an engineer, you may feel like your skills aren’t commanding the premium they once did. Many engineers have faced layoffs or restructuring. But even for those of us who still have jobs, something corrosive is happening. You may have heard some version of this:

“ChatGPT answered that in five seconds. Why can’t you?”

Or, “I made this app in a weekend. Why is our team taking so long?”

I worked on a team where leadership said things like this directly to engineers. This was in 2024 and 2025, when the AI craze was in full swing and Claude and ChatGPT adoption was rising.

Generative AI (and the marketing behind it) gives people the illusion that the work is simpler than it is. A working demo hides complexity, and once someone has a website that works, they may decide they no longer need engineers, or start to distrust the ones they do have.

Some CEOs want to believe they can replace an engineering team with a few sexy prompts. Many companies also want them to believe this.

That website works great in the demo—under specific conditions and without users with thumbs for fingers. Then it has to plug into a system with millions of lines of old code, satisfy legal requirements, meet accessibility standards, and be delivered in a complex deployment process.

Thinking that writing code was the only bottleneck for deploying new software is like the Titanic seeing the tip of the iceberg and assuming there was nothing underneath it.

Engineers have a unique position in the AI space, because you have the capacity to understand how these models work much better than the average person. Use this to your advantage.

Learn how AI models work. If you can’t already explain that LLMs are probabilistic, what tokens are, or why training data matters, spend a weekend fixing that. You don’t need to become a full-blown AI researcher. A few fundamentals will put you ahead of most people making the AI decisions.

Teach upward. Turn that knowledge into teaching moments for the people who lead you. Explain the limits of these tools, and why a demo and a production system are different animals. It keeps people from truly believing that a notebook full of prompts can replace an engineering team.

Consider the criticism of today’s processes. Some of what we do has been treated as ceremony for too long. Be willing to say, “you know what, maybe you’re right, this process is too slow for the speed we can work at now.” Conceding that earns you the credibility to defend the steps that matter.

I still believe that speed at the cost of everything else is harmful—but that’s a topic for another time.

Find your voice. Engineers at the forefront of AI adoption need to push back and explain why we do things the way we do. Nobody else in the room is going to do it for us.

Your goal, in my opinion, is to save your organization from buying into the hype so much that they chase the wrong thing. Our job, before and after AI, is building safe and useful products for human beings, and engineers are still best suited for that.

The need to educate engineering students about ethics and social responsibility is widely recognized, but today’s curricula often miss the mark. Three professors propose a new approach: adding ethics training directly to core technical coursework.

Looking for a career in quantum computing hardware? An IBM spin-off called Anderon could receive up to $1 billion in funding from the U.S. CHIPS and Science Act for its quantum foundry, established earlier this year. Could Anderon do for quantum hardware what TSMC did for conventional chips?

When Gurmeet Saran joined Anthropic’s technical staff in 2025, he entered a role focused on a key question: How do you know whether you can trust a chatbot like Claude? Learn more about Saran’s path and his work at the AI company.

Brian Jenney is the owner of Parsity, an online education platform that helps people break into AI and modern software roles through project-based learning and one-on-one mentorship with senior developers. Parsity helps career changers transition into software by focusing on practical skills, real-world systems, and the kind of experience companies actually look for.Outside Parsity, Brian works a senior software engineer in the SF Bay Area.Brian is also a father of three, and when he’s not working with students or building programs, you might catch him running around Lake Merritt in Oakland, California.

What was wrong with the headline "Engineering Jobs That AI Can't Replace"?

Different headlines appear in different places for stories. Not seeing it on the article doesn't mean that the headline appeared differently somewhere else.

#3234. Unfold CEO Ran Cherniavsky on breaking down enterprise data barriers to AI adoption

As enterprises accelerate AI adoption, a major obstacle remains: much of the data AI needs is still trapped inside legacy systems, proprietary software, and applications that lack modern interfaces. Traditional integration tools have helped connect enterprise systems, but they often cannot access the full scope of information or capture the business context needed to make that data useful.

For Ran Cherniavsky, CEO and Co-Founder of Unfold, the solution is to rethink how enterprises access their data. Unfold works through the interfaces businesses already use, extracting information and mapping the underlying logic without requiring system replacements or disruptive migrations.

In this Q&A, Cherniavsky discusses why data accessibility is becoming a defining challenge for enterprise AI, how Unfold unlocks information from otherwise closed systems, and what becomes possible when AI agents can finally understand the full picture of an organization’s operations.

Because integration was built for systems, not for AI. It connected system A to system B, one field at a time, through whatever the vendor chose to expose. AI needs access to everything a human being can see in a system, and an understanding of what it means. And it needs it fast, without a project for every field. That’s a different problem.

Companies that can’t put AI on their core data will fall behind the ones that can, and that gap opens fast.

The costs show up long before that. Companies pay specialized consultants, year after year, to map a system’s fields by hand. Analysts pull capped reports manually and stitch them together in Excel. AI pilots stall because the model only sees the slice the API exposes, and gets the answers wrong. In effect, you’re renting access to your own data through someone else’s UI.

And there’s a risk you can’t see: if nobody can read what’s inside a system, nobody can be confident it’s secure either. You’re left hoping.

AI adoption, and it’s not close. That’s where the pressure from the board is, and that’s where locked data costs you right now. You can’t just open Claude and ask, “A dealership owner can’t ask Claude how old the warranty money owed to him is, because that data is stuck behind reports?” Not because you can’t write the question in plain English, but because the data isn’t accessible.

Security and modernization feel the same problem, but differently. Security is a symptom: you can’t secure what you can’t see. Modernization is the long way around. According to Gartner, 45% of core systems still run on mainframes or on-prem client/server, and 34% of organizations now leave core applications as they are because modernizing them is too risky. AI can’t wait for that to change.

Solve access and context for AI, and you’ve solved a big part of the other two along the way.

The same way a person does. Employees don’t work with a system only through its API. They use the UI, reports, exports, files and more. Unfold works through every interface the application exposes, with or without an API.

Our team spent years doing deep software research, integrating with systems regardless of what they exposed. That used to take months per system, by hand. With AI, Unfold becomes the subject-matter expert on a system in days, maps where every piece of data lives and how it moves, and then builds a deterministic read-only collector that gets it out through the system’s own permissions.

That works on mainframes like AS/400, on-prem ERPs, and modern SaaS that only exposes part of its data. If a system has a UI or a command line, we can work with it. Onboarding takes up to 14 days, for any system.

Raw data without meaning is noise. In Oracle’s ERP JD Edwards, tables carry numbers instead of names. A status field holds a code nobody remembers defining. Two systems call the same customer by different names.

Unfold learns each system the way a trained employee would: what each object means, how objects relate, which business rules and exceptions apply, and how people actually use it. Because we see the screen and what sits underneath it, we can tie what a user sees in the UI to where it lives in the data.

That knowledge used to live with SMEs, implementation partners and vendors, and much of it walked out the door. We rebuild it as a catalog of every data object, with its business meaning and its full journey through the system. AI gets the data and the context together, and stops guessing.

Once each system is understood, we connect them. The same customer is KUNNR in SAP and an Account in Salesforce. The same site has a different ID in each ERP. Unfold maps all of it into one canonical enterprise schema, so data from every system arrives normalized and consistent.

Governance is built in from the start. The data stays with the customer, in their own source systems. Lineage comes with it, because we know where every field came from and how it was transformed.

And the collectors are deterministic: the same question returns the same data every time. That’s what you need before you let an agent act on it.

First, we don’t replace data platforms; we feed them. Splunk, Snowflake and Databricks are where data gets searched, analyzed and put to work by AI, and they’re only as good as what reaches them. Today, that’s whatever a source system’s API or export allows. And you don’t have to move the data at all: Unfold can work with it where it lives, in the source systems, or deliver it straight to agents through our connector to Claude, Gemini and others.

Unfold sits upstream. We get the data and the logic out of the systems that never fed those platforms, with the meaning attached, and deliver it wherever the customer needs it: their lake, their warehouse or their agents. At a global retailer, point-of-sale data from an AS/400 mainframe is heading into a Gemini Enterprise fraud-detection agent. At a manufacturer, plant control system data is heading into a CMDB.

Traditional integration starts from a catalog of prebuilt connectors and moves what each vendor exposes, one project at a time. Unfold starts from the system itself: every interface, the full data model and the business context, in days rather than months.

The best use cases start the same way: someone sees data in a screen and can’t get it into the workflow they need. A few examples:

A global retailer needs point-of-sale data from AS/400 systems in more than ten countries feeding its fraud detection, which now runs on Gemini Enterprise. One country’s regulator told them to stop selling until that control was in place.

A top-10 US insurer pays contractors with specialized expertise to map claims-system fields to the database by hand. Then another team of engineers comes in to build the ETL. All of that takes weeks. We do it automatically, in days.

A multi-store auto dealership group had its parts, service and warranty data locked behind reports in its dealership management system.

Now the owner asks, in plain English, “How old is the warranty money owed to us?”

Customers measure value in three ways: time (days instead of months), cost (consultants, professional services and engineering they no longer need), and outcomes that weren’t possible before, like an answer across systems, or a business that keeps selling.

By not touching them. Unfold doesn’t require code changes or a migration. It works with the system as it is, through the interfaces that are already there, and read only, by design.

That matters because modernizing core systems is risky, and everyone knows it. Gartner finds that 34% of organizations now leave core applications as they are for exactly that reason, up from 16% in 2023, and that 40% of the modernizations needed for autonomous business will be late by 2030.

So instead of waiting years for a replacement, you get the data and the business logic out today and put AI to work on top of it. And when you modernize, you already have a full map of what the old system holds and what it means, which is a big part of the migration work.

AI adoption stops crawling and starts running. Today, enterprises work for AI: teams spend months on integrations just to feed it data. Once every system is open and understood, that flips. We work with AI, and AI does the integrations and runs the workflows itself.

Agents stop guessing and start working on the real business. Most agents today reach email, documents and a few SaaS APIs. The core of the business, the orders, claims, inventory, warranty and plant operations, lives elsewhere.

Open that up, and a dealership owner asks one question across parts, service and warranty. A fraud model sees point-of-sale data from every country. A finance team gets on-time-in-full numbers across two ERPs that use different IDs for the same site.

Then it compounds. Agents follow a process end to end, like order-to-cash, across every system it touches, instead of stopping at the edge of one. That’s when AI moves from answering questions to running the business.

It already is. Gartner says that through 2030, the biggest compounding challenge for agentic AI is data access and control. Models keep getting smarter, but more intelligence alone won’t move the enterprise. Models need the enterprise’s proprietary data, and the context of how each system is used.

How to overcome it: start from the business outcome, not from a data project. Pick one AI initiative that’s blocked by a system you can’t get data out of, solve it, and expand system by system on the same layer. Stop treating access as a string of one-off integrations, and don’t wait for modernization to finish.

And treat the knowledge inside your systems as an asset. The people who understood those systems are retiring or gone. Capturing that context now is part of being AI-ready.

History tends to follow the same path. First we invent something. Then we find a commercial way to use it. Only years later does it actually change how we live. The first modern car came in 1886, but it took decades to transform society.

That time went into building the infrastructure around it: roads, gas stations, bridges. AI is at that same point today. We have probably the most powerful engine we’ve ever built, and the models keep getting better. But the transformation inside enterprises hasn’t happened yet, and the reason isn’t intelligence. The roads aren’t there.

Integration is a big part of those roads, and it was built for a different kind of traffic. It connected systems to systems with connectors and pipes, moving one field at a time. Over the next three to five years, the traffic changes. AI is now the one that needs the data, and AI needs all of it, along with what it means.

So I think the market splits. Moving data becomes a commodity, like a basic road. The value moves to the layer that understands the enterprise: full access to every system, the business context behind it, and one schema across all of them.

Gartner already treats AI context platforms as a separate market, growing from $28B in 2026 to $78B by 2030. It also notes that these platforms are limited by how much they can actually get out of systems of record. That’s exactly the gap we fill.

The difference this time is that we don’t have to wait 40 years. With AI, enterprises can build the roads much faster than they built them for the car, but only if their data can actually reach the engine. Our goal is to lead this category and become the knowledge foundation for enterprise AI, so that every AI use case in the enterprise runs on Unfold, from the mainframe to SaaS.

Our team spent years doing deep software research, getting data out of systems that were never designed to give it up. Then AI arrived, and suddenly every company had the same problem we’d been solving by hand, at a scale nobody could staff. Twenty years ago, your data sat on your own servers.

Today it sits behind vendors, interfaces, and knowledge that’s retiring. We built Unfold so AI can understand any enterprise system the way a long-time employee does. The long-term vision is simple: every AI use case in the enterprise runs on Unfold, from the mainframe to SaaS.

#3233. ‘Awkwafina: The Unlikely Cook’ premieres on Apple TV

Defined by Apple TV as its newest “culinary adventure” show, ‘Awkwafina: The Unlikely Cook’ is now streaming on the platform.

Starring and executive-produced by Emmy-winning actor and comedian Nora Lum, aka Awkwafina (The Farewell), the show will run for eight episodes through December 18, and it will feature “acclaimed chefs, restaurateurs and her characterful family.”

Here’s Apple TV’s synopsis of ‘Awkwafina: The Unlikely Cook’:

In the series, Nora embarks on a deeply personal cross-country journey as she explores contemporary Asian American cuisine, starting with her family’s remarkable legacy. Nora’s family ran Lum’s, the iconic Cantonese restaurant in Flushing, New York, and the very first in a now thriving Chinatown. But despite growing up in the family business, she can’t cook. At all. She could ruin an instant ramen. (…) With help from acclaimed chefs, restaurateurs and her characterful family, she travels the country to explore what it takes to master Asian food in the kitchen and whether she will ultimately reimagine Lum’s legacy for today.

‘Awkwafina: The Unlikely Cook’ joins Apple TV’s growing catalog of food-centric shows, including ‘Omnivore’ and ‘Knife Edge: Chasing Michelin Stars.’ It also marks the second collaboration between Apple TV and production company Twofour, following the Emmy-nominated travel series ‘The Reluctant Traveler With Eugene Levy.’

#3232. From Chip Lab to Center Stage

This integrated circuit designer explains wearables to consumers

Joanna Goodrich is the associate editor of The Institute.

IEEE Member Preethi Ashwath is one of the few women who work in analog integrated circuit design, where about 11 percent are female.

Many engineers are more comfortable working behind the scenes developing technology than speaking to consumers about products. But Preethi Ashwath has learned to take center stage, talking about the “hearable” and wearable devices she has had a hand in developing as an analog integrated circuit designer in the consumer electronics division at Analog Devices of Wilmington, Mass.

The IEEE member is one of the few women who work in the specialized field, where about 11 percent are female, according to career platform Zippia.

Preethi Ashwath Employer Analog Devices, in BostonTitle Integrated circuit designerMember grade MemberAlma maters SJB Institute of Technology in Bengaluru, India; University of California, Irvine

SJB Institute of Technology in Bengaluru, India; University of California, Irvine

Ashwath stepped out from behind the scenes last year to meet with attendees at the Consumer Electronics Show (CES) in Las Vegas. She demonstrated Analog’s new earbuds, which track people’s heart and lung health through vibrations in their ear canals.

After she demonstrated her ability to explain the technology to consumers in simple terms, Analog selected her to represent the company at other events. She says she has “come to see speaking as part of contributing to the field, rather than something separate from technical work.”

She also gives technical talks on various aspects of electrostatic discharge (ESD) and other topics, as well as participates in panel discussions, she says, because they “reach engineers well beyond my immediate team.”

Ashwath is an active volunteer with the IEEE Circuits and Systems Society.

“Whether through designing semiconductor products, publishing technical articles, reviewing conference papers, or speaking at industry events, I try to contribute to the growth of the engineering community and the advancement of the field,” she says.

Ashwath, who grew up in Bengaluru, India, learned about electronics engineering from her high school physics tutor.

That introduction led her to take electronics as one of her core courses in her final years there. At the time, Ashwath’s older sister was pursuing an engineering degree.

“Between my interest in electronics and seeing her already on that path, it became clear to me that engineering was the way to go,” Ashwath says.

After earning a bachelor’s degree in electronics and communications engineering at the SJB Institute of Technology, in Bengaluru, she wanted to pursue a career in very-large-scale integration. But that changed once she moved to the United States and began her master’s program in electrical engineering at the University of California, Irvine.

She discovered her passion for circuits and devices during an internship at Intel in Santa Clara, Calif. She learned about circuit design, package design, and reliability verification tools such as Ansys Totem.

“Seeing every layer of the chip development process gave me a more complete picture of what goes into building a semiconductor product,” she says. “Through that experience, I realized I felt most connected to design.

“It was the hard work and creativity that drew me in. You start with a specification, build a circuit, simulate it, then wait for the chip to come back from fabrication. When your design works, it’s a real feeling of satisfaction. It teaches you patience and perseverance.”

After attaining her master’s degree, she was hired by Intel as an analog design engineer. She gained experience in mixed-signal circuit design before joining Analog. In her current role, she works on consumer hearables such as earbuds and wearables including fitness trackers and health monitors.

Her main focus is designing ESD pad rings, the borders of specialized circuits built around a microchip’s outermost edge to protect it from the discharge, which can damage circuit paths or introduce latent defects that lead to failures later in the chip’s life cycle.

“On a chip with multiple voltage domains, you have to plan how the protection structures are placed and connected across the whole pad ring—and get it right,” Ashwath says. “A mistake there could cause a chip to fail in the field in ways that are very hard to debug afterward.

“It’s detailed work that requires understanding both the device physics and how the whole chip fits together.”

Part of the job is designing and creating an integrated circuit’s building blocks, including ESD protection structures and other mixed-signal blocks. Ashwath conducts rigorous checks to verify they work as intended before being integrated into a chip.

She collaborates with ESD advisors, layout designers, and the digital team that designs the chip’s digital logic.

“I work with them to make sure my analog circuits and their digital blocks work together correctly,” she says. “No two days look exactly the same.”

In 2024 she was recognized with the company’s Impact Award for her “exceptional work on a critical project with significant cross-functional business impact.”

Ashwath was selected to represent Analog at events after a senior leader encouraged her to ask for high-visibility opportunities, she says.

“Most of my time is spent on designing circuits and simulations,” she says. “At CES, I stood in front of customers, engineers, and members of the press, explaining our technology and answering questions on the spot.”

The earbuds she demonstrated monitor minute vibrations from a user’s heart and lungs, according to the Analog website. The vibrations can detect arrhythmia, a leaky heart valve, or fluid in the lungs.

“Hearables are evolving from playing back audio to becoming health-monitoring platforms,” she says. “The ear turns out to be a good location for picking up physiological signals, so these devices can capture vital signs while someone is simply wearing them normally.

“The hard part is achieving high signal quality. The signals you’re trying to detect are very small and buried in the noise from the person’s movements and the surrounding environment.

“That’s where analog front-end design becomes critical. Extracting a meaningful signal from a noisy real-world environment is fundamentally an analog problem.”

Being face-to-face with customers at the conference was new to her.

“What struck me most was seeing how people react to the technology,” she says. “When you’re designing a block, you’re focused on specifications and margins. At CES, after explaining what the product does, I had a better understanding of why it matters to them.

“That connection between the circuit work and the final product is something you don’t always see from the design bench.”

Since the CES, Ashwath has presented other technologies she’s worked on. At the annual National Association of Music Merchants show in Anaheim, Calif., she demonstrated the A2B Automotive Audio Bus to the audio industry. The bus uses a low-cost unshielded twisted-pair cable to carry multichannel digital audio, control data, synchronized clock signals, and power in fewer than 50 microseconds, according to Analog.

“IEEE connects you with academia, which you don’t get much exposure to once you’re in industry. That connection between industry and academic work is valuable in both directions.”

At the company’s Global Technology Conference—an internal event held in Boston that draws engineers from the company’s more than 50 sites around the world—Ashwath led a demonstration of its solutions for augmented reality smart glasses.

“Each of these events has a different audience,” she says. “Learning to explain my technical work to different people has become a skill I’ve acquired.”

The most rewarding part of her job, she says, is seeing the end result of her work.

“You spend months on a design, and there’s a long wait between finishing it and finding out whether your instincts were right,” she says. “When the measurements match what you simulated, that’s the most satisfying moment in this job.

“The other part is knowing my work ends up in a real product. The circuits I design go into devices people actually use every day.”

Like many engineers, Ashwath joined IEEE to access research published in the IEEE Xplore Digital Library. It keeps her current in a field that keeps moving, she says.

During her first year of membership, in 2021, she discovered other perks including networking and educational opportunities.

“IEEE connects you to a community outside your own company,” she says. “Attending lectures and technical talks exposes you to approaches and problems you wouldn’t encounter in your own work.”

She eventually began seeking out volunteer opportunities, specifically with IEEE conferences and journals, because they are “how you stay current with what’s happening in circuits and systems beyond your own day-to-day work,” she says.

“As an analog designer,” she says, “being connected to that broader community matters. The field moves, and you need a way to keep learning from it.”

She serves as a peer reviewer of papers for several IEEE conferences including the IEEE International Symposium on Circuits and Systems and the IEEE International Midwest Symposium on Circuits and Systems. ISCAS is the flagship conference of the IEEE Circuits and Systems Society. MWSCAS is the oldest U.S. conference on the technologies.

“Someone has to assess whether submitted work is technically sound and worth presenting,” she says, “and that only happens if practicing engineers are willing to put in the time.”

The combination of learning from the community and contributing to it is what makes her membership worthwhile, she says.

“Analog design is a field where you’re always learning. Just when you feel you understand one architecture, there’s another one to learn,” she says. “Being an active learner isn’t optional in this field; it’s the requirement, and being part of the IEEE community helps with that.

“IEEE also connects you with academia, which you don’t get much exposure to once you’re in industry.

“Reviewing papers means reading what researchers are working on, which is often quite different from how the same problems get approached in a product environment. That connection between industry and academic work is valuable in both directions.”

Joanna Goodrich is the associate editor of The Institute, covering the work and accomplishments of IEEE members and IEEE and technology-related events. She has a master's degree in health communications from Rutgers University, in New Brunswick, N.J.

#3231. Apple confirms $7.5 billion bond sale following strong investor demand

Following yesterday’s report that Apple was preparing to raise approximately $7 billion through a bond offering, the company has now finalized terms with the SEC, confirming a slightly larger amount. Here are the details.

Yesterday morning, Apple filed a preliminary prospectus with the SEC, outlining plans to issue a series of bonds maturing between 2028 and 2036.

Soon after, Bloomberg reported that the bond sale was targeting roughly $7 billion, with investor interest already surpassing $30 billion.

Now, Apple has filed the final pricing term sheet for the bond sale with the SEC, confirming a $7.5 billion offering across the seven previously announced series, with the following breakdown:

Floating-rate bonds, as the name implies, have interest rates that fluctuate over time based on certain market conditions, rather than remaining fixed.

Of that $7.5 billion, Apple expects to receive approximately $7.47 billion after deducting underwriting discounts and other offering expenses.

In essence, Apple will pay investors interest over the life of the bonds, then repay the full amount borrowed when each series reaches maturity. Apple may also choose to repay some or all of its fixed-rate bonds early.

As described in yesterday’s prospectus, the company intends to use the proceeds for “general corporate purposes,” which may include stock buybacks, dividends, acquisitions, and debt repayment.

#3230. UnitedHealth shares are doing something unusual ahead of earnings

The only thing more expensive than health insurance is perhaps the costs of insuring shares of health insurers. Case in point: UnitedHealth Group, which reports earnings Tuesday.

Implied volatility is running at twice realized volatility ahead of the October 13 quarterly earnings release. In other words, options prices - the cost of insuring the underlying stock - are expensive, which sets up well for short premium strategies.

In the case of UnitedHealth shares, traders can sell November premium to cut the cost of a longer-dated January call by more than half. UnitedHealth heads into Tuesday's report with much of the damage from its prior missteps already priced in. While rising healthcare costs always remain a headwind, management's 13% to 16% EPS growth target looks achievable. The stock has basically been flat over the last five years.

By the way, according to the company, 90% of United's 52 million customers worldwide are in the U.S. By its own statistics, the company covers about 12% to 13.5% of the U.S. population.

Growing enrollment is critical to EPS growth, but so too is underwriting margin. In the managed care and health insurance business, underwriting margin represents the core operational profitability generated directly from managing healthcare risk. It measures the financial return an insurer achieves strictly from collecting premiums and managing medical care. On the enrollment side, ACA marketplace-driven enrollment appears poised to decline, a headwind for revenue in a segment that had been a growth driver. Fortunately, it's a smaller piece of the enterprise than Medicare and Commercial. Commercial fee-based enrollment grew ~2.9% YoY between 2024 and 2025, while total Medicare enrollment grew 4.5%. The commercial segment growth may not look impressive as a headline number, but given the U.S. workforce grew ~1.4% over the same period, United appears to be gaining market share.

At 17 times forward earnings, and with free cash flow at 5.7% of enterprise value and 6.5% of market cap, the stock isn't priced for any recovery. On the options side, the market is implying 40% volatility for a stock that's been realizing 20%. Granted. The 40% number captures this week's earnings, and it's likely elevated because the stock has had a couple of eye-watering earnings moves in the past 8 reported quarters. In January, the stock fell almost 20% following earnings, and April 2025 saw a similar sharp decline.

As it stands, UNH is about 12-13% below the midpoint of the two-year high and low. The stock has traded lower in five of the last 8 earnings. Current options prices imply a 6.5% earnings move, according to Cboe LiveVol data. That's the second highest implied move in almost two years.

Sell the November 340/420 strangle to help finance the purchase of the January 2027 400 call. Buying the Jan 400 call costs $18.20. Selling the Nov 420 call at $5.80 and the Nov 340 put at $4.80 brings in $10.60, for a net debit of about $7.60, cutting the call's cost by roughly 58%. If UNH finishes November between 340 and 420, both short legs expire worthless and the January call is held for $7.60, with a breakeven of $407.60 at January expiration. A rally through 420 is covered by the long 400 call. The real risk is below: a close under 340 means buying shares there, for an effective basis near $347.60 including the debit.

#3229. Twelve South’s new Cablesnap charger has a built-in retractable USB-C cable

Popular Apple accessory maker Twelve South is launching a new retractable Cablesnap 65W travel charger this week. It has a built-in USB-C cable, alongside an additional USB-C port and USB-A port.

You can order the new Cablesnap 65W on Amazon today for $49.99.

We’ve seen travel chargers with retractable cables before, and Twelve South’s is similar. It has a 29-inch (75cm) spring-loaded USB-C cable built right in, so you can pull out exactly as much as you need. Then, when you’re ready to pack up, just give it a little pull, and it snaps back into the charging brick.

In addition to the retractable USB-C cable, there’s a separate USB-C port and a USB-A port for charging other accessories. It can charge at up to 65W speeds, shared across each connected device.

#3228. CoreWeave asks Texas governor-elect to let permitted data centres finish

CEO Michael Intrator wrote to Gina Hinojosa, who campaigned to pause new data centres in the state.

I cloud company CoreWeave has written to Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, offering to work with her team on data centre rules. The letter from chief executive Michael Intrator was sent on Saturday, Bloomberg reported.

Intrator offered to work with her transition team on finishing projects that already have permits. He also offered help setting clear, lasting standards for new ones, Bloomberg reported.

Hinojosa, a Democrat, won Tuesday’s election after promising to pause new data centres until the state has rules for them. She has said they should pay their own way and put Texans’ water and power first, ABC13 reported.

CoreWeave appears to expect that projects already approved can go ahead. Carl Holshouser, its head of government affairs, said in a LinkedIn post that Hinojosa had made clear permitted projects can be completed.

TNW could not find Hinojosa saying this herself. Her team has not said how a pause would work.

Holshouser, who helped write the letter, said families should not pay for new power lines and plants. He added that new sites should protect local water and power.

Texas has already got tougher. In August, outgoing Governor Greg Abbott ordered regulators to pause new grid links and start auditing data centres.

This odd-looking variation on a basic move is surprisingly effective

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Spare a thought for the push-up, that most humble of body-weight exercises, and almost certainly the best known. It is as simple as exercise gets — lie on the floor, support your weight with your arms, lower to the ground, push back up, and repeat — it can be done almost anywhere and it is hugely effective, building strength and definition in the arms, chest, and shoulders. It also works the core, if you’re doing it properly. And if you want to challenge yourself, just do a few more. It is, I would suggest, a perfect exercise. And why mess with perfection? On the other hand, why not?

Which brings me neatly to the Hindu push-up, a dynamic variation on the basic move. It’s not new, having been a core training move for Indian wrestlers since at least the 19th century. Ghulam Mohammad Baksh Butt, an undefeated giant of the sport (he was known, deservedly, as The Great Gama) purportedly did 3,000 Hindu push-ups every day as part of his savage training regimen.

The basic push-up is hard for beginners and even if you do them regularly, adding reps is tough, but the Hindu push-up is much harder, so I would not recommend this move for newcomers. However, if you’re up for it, it will improve your flexibility and work your back, glutes and legs in addition to the benefits listed above. If you do Pilates or yoga, you will probably find this a little more comfortable, in terms of form, at least.

I am inherently suspicious of any move that involves or is adjacent to yoga, as I am not nearly as flexible as I’d like to be, but I’ve been doing pushups for as long as I’ve been exercising (as with most people, I imagine, it was the first body-weight move I ever attempted — thanks, Dad).

For that reason, I approached this challenge with a mixture of confidence and trepidation, which is enormously confusing. I suspected I’d be undone by the inverted V and end cobra position, but I found I could do both reasonably well. What got me was the incredible strain it put on my arms, which was also what impressed me.

On day one, I struggled mightily with the movement from downward dog and was inclined to come up too early, which put a strain on my lower back. Bad idea. I restarted, going more slowly. This made for better form but an astonishing level of stress on my triceps as I swept down and then up into the cobra position, or as close as I could get to it.

Afterwards, I felt the effort in my arms, across my shoulders, and, to a lesser extent, in my lower back (in a good way). I managed two sets of 10, with some wobbling towards the end of each set. I strongly recommend you use a mat for this move, as your feet will slide back on a bare floor. When I finished, my triceps let me know someone had been working them in a way they did not recognize.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The following day, I still had the not displeasing ache in my triceps, which I do not feel after traditional push-ups (mind you, I could just add more reps). This time, I worked on controlling the downward and upward movement, rather than the weight-bearing part of the move. I kept my elbows close to my sides (do not let them flare out) and completed three sets of 10. Obviously, I had not become stronger after one day, so this considerable improvement was entirely down to better form.

For the rest of the week, I continued to pay close attention to my form. If you begin in the high inverted V position, your arms will not be too far forward when you sweep down, which will make things easier. Not easy. Easier. Very slightly easier. I began to enjoy the effort and the flowing motion when things were going well.

That said, I never went beyond three sets of 12 — this is a difficult, challenging move and I would only recommend it if you’re already very comfortable doing regular push-ups and have no lower back issues (you might want to check with a medical professional before you try the Hindu pushup). But if you do feel you are ready, then I can heartily recommend this exercise.

By the end of the week, I was feeling it across my chest, as well as in my upper arms and shoulders, and I was more than happy to be adding some flexibility work to a strength move. The ache in my muscles stayed with me for the week, which suggested the move continued to work my arms and chest in a way regular push-ups do not. I won’t be doing 3,000 of these every day, but that’s only because I have no desire to preface my name with The Great. I’ll settle for The Didn’t Fall On His Face…

#3224. Build a Hidden Lock With a Magnetic Imager

Stephen Cass is the special projects editor at IEEE Spectrum.

Only a programmable secret gesture with a magnet can open this lockbox. (Or a hammer. It’s a proof of concept.)

Like many a nerd, I have a certain fascination with locks. This originates in reading the memoir Surely You’re Joking, Mr. Feynman as a teenager, in which Richard Feynman recounts picking locks and cracking combinations while at his day job working on the Manhattan Project at Los Alamos. I currently have a couple of locksport pick sets and training locks that I purchased at hacker conferences over the years (although I’m still terrible at it), and I delight in the YouTube exploits of folks like the LockPickingLawyer.

All of which left me wondering if I could try building an interesting lock. One dodge that lockmakers have long used to challenge would-be plunderers is to conceal the existence of the lock itself. A modern variant of this is the magnetic lock, where a magnet is held or slid against an innocuous portion of a door or box, releasing a catch. The problem with this is that, once you guess the location of the lock, any strong magnet will open it.

So I started thinking about embedding an RFID reader under the surface and resigning myself to keeping track of yet another access card. But then I stumbled across something much more interesting: SparkFun’s US $100 magnetic imaging tile. I realized I could use this to build a magnetic lock that opens with a programmable secret gesture.

I used a few discrete components to drive the servo motor and put the lock into program mode [top], controlled by a Teensy 4.1 microcontroller [middle]. An array of Hall-effect sensors detect magnetic fields [bottom].James Provost

The magnetic imaging tile is a small-run SparkFun board based on the work of Peter Jansen. It features an 8-by-8 grid of Hall-effect sensors, and uses an SPI interface to talk to the microcontroller of your choice. These sensors can detect both the magnitude and polarity of a magnetic field, and the board can report its measurements hundreds to thousands of times per second, depending on how much processing power your microcontroller has available. This is easily fast enough to capture the motion of a magnet being moved by hand across the board’s sensor area—my secret gesture.

An interesting thing about using magnetic fields is that if I was in extreme paranoia mode, I could shield the entire lock behind copper sheeting, something I couldn’t do with an RFID reader. The copper sheet would act as a Faraday cage, blocking any RFID signal, along with any other electromagnetic fields an attacker with an EMF meter might use to locate the lock.

I chose a Teensy 4.1 as my microcontroller. I like the Teensy because it offers loads of input/output, a 600-megahertz processor, a megabyte of RAM, and a built-in SD card, all in a slim package with an equally slim $32 price tag.

Wiring the Teensy to the magnetic-imaging tile was trivial, only complicated by the fact that one side of the board has a silk-screen error that misidentifies the SPI connections (SparkFun says this will be fixed in future runs of the board).

In extreme paranoia mode, I could shield the entire lock behind copper sheeting.

To create the gesture-recognition software, I once again turned to vibe coding. If you read my Hands On piece in the April 2026 issue of IEEE Spectrum on creating a teletext suite for ham radio, you’ll know I’ve been grappling with how vibe coding should be used in DIY projects, if at all. So this time, instead of letting Claude write all the software, I confined it to writing just two support libraries, which you can find in our online repository at https://github.com/IEEESpectrumHandsOn.

One library is in charge of recording a lock gesture and saving it to the Teensy’s nonvolatile storage. The other library monitors the tile and reports whether or not a newly detected gesture passes a selectable threshold to be considered a match.

I wrote the top-level code myself to keep it as DIY as possible. This code handles things like a button that puts the system in gesture-recording mode after a brief delay, the indicator LED for recording mode, and the code that operates the physical locking mechanism.

Hall-effect sensors rely on a current passing through a p-type slab of silicon. A magnetic field passing through the silicon deflects charge carriers toward the edges of the slab, creating a voltage proportional to the field [left]. By looking at the intensities of the voltages across an 8-by-8 grid of sensors, the microcontroller can reconstruct a gesture [right]. James Provost

Of course, I needed something to lock to demonstrate my proof of concept. I bought a wooden craft box and removed the existing lid latch. I glued a notched beam inside the lid and built a mechanism that uses a servo motor to rotate another beam in and out of this notch. I will be the first to admit this mechanism goes beyond “simple” and into “simplistic,” but it’s sufficiently robust for my demo. The box has ample room for the magnetic imaging tile to be mounted against one wall, along with the Teensy and other supporting electronics. These include a battery pack, the recording button, and a small additional board with two NPN transistors. These convert the Teensy’s 3.3-volt control signals to a 5-V signal needed to drive the servo.

Once it was all put together, I soon discovered that the small size of the magnetic tile’s sensing area—just 3 centimeters square—made it easy to fit the tile inside the box but hard to do the unlock gesture on the outside so that it is read correctly. Marking the outline of the sensor area on the outside defeated the point of having a hidden lock, so instead I once again turned to mining my Irish heritage. I created a Celtic knotwork pattern that runs in a band across the front of the lockbox (I used an online knotwork generator and then projected and traced the pattern onto the box). Using the pattern as a camouflaged reference grid I can make a repeatable gesture within the confines of the sensor area. (To make the gestures I’m using a magnetic stylus borrowed from a ferrite core-memory kit we featured in 2022.)

There’s obvious room for improvement in any more serious installation. The biggest drawback currently is that if the box is locked when the battery runs out, you can’t open it again without breaking something. This could be solved by adding a hidden inductive charging coil. Nonetheless, the demo lockbox works well—now I just have to think what I should store in it!

Stephen Cass is the special projects editor at IEEE Spectrum. He currently helms Spectrum's Hands On column, and is also responsible for interactive projects such as the Top Programming Languages app. He has a bachelor's degree in experimental physics from Trinity College Dublin.

#3221. IEEE Xplore Digital Library Adds AI Assistant

The search tool offers summaries and verifiable source links

Claire Olini is the senior manager for IEEE Corporate and Strategic Product Launch and Engagement.

Michael Spada is director of IEEE Product Launch and Engagement Strategy.

IEEE recently released the IEEE Xplore AI Research Suite, built on the full text of millions of peer-reviewed publications in the IEEE Xplore Digital Library. The library offers full-text access to IEEE standards, journals, magazines, conference proceedings, and more.

Researchers who use the AI suite to search the digital library receive answers grounded in verified scientific results, ensuring a high level of accuracy and trust.

Powered by a proprietary AI system optimized for STEM literature, the suite introduces powerful, intelligent features within the digital library. The suite enables users to seamlessly search and discover articles to accelerate their comprehension of complex technical papers.

The system surfaces deep insights, replacing the typical keyword queries with natural, conversational research workflows.

As AI tools become more common in conducting research, IEEE collaborated to build the suite around a simple principle: Answers should be trustworthy, not just fast, says W. Clem Karl, vice president, IEEE Publication Services and Products.

“AI can be a highly effective and beneficial tool that can help researchers accelerate discovery, enhance decision-making, and surface new connections,” Karl says. “However, many AI engines present a great risk of hallucinating answers or introducing bias into otherwise credible research. With this in mind, IEEE has taken a responsible approach in our AI strategy by developing concrete safeguards to ensure our solution is rigorously grounded in scientific evidence that users can trust.

“As stewards of the scholarly record, we held the new AI engine to the same standards as the peer-reviewed research we publish: A researcher shouldn’t have to trust an answer; they should be able to verify the work behind it.”

The IEEE Xplore AI Research Suite was developed in close collaboration with global scientific and library communities.

The development process began with research into user needs and the challenges associated with existing AI research assistants. More than 3,000 testers—including engineers, scientists, and library information professionals—provided feedback to refine the AI engine and support research workflows.

To mitigate the risk of AI hallucinations, the search-retrieval process is limited to querying the millions of IEEE peer-reviewed full-text documents, alongside an expertly curated dataset of STEM metadata. If the AI tool is unable to find relevant scientific content within the defined dataset, it is designed to inform the user rather than generate fabricated answers.

“IEEE is committed to providing the technical community with a highly precise and reliable research experience,” says Steven Heffner, IEEE’s chief publication officer and managing director of IEEE Publications. “The IEEE Xplore AI Research Suite offers something unique in that it is the only AI research assistant that leverages both the full-text and metadata of IEEE’s peer-reviewed content, rather than abstracts alone.

“The difference is significant: Our internal testing showed a threefold increase in result quality and accuracy across every key metric. These results underscore how critical full-text grounding is for technical research.”

For more information about features and coverage, or to request a demo for your organization, visit the IEEE Xplore AI Research Suite website.

Claire Olini is the senior manager for IEEE Corporate and Strategic Product Launch and Engagement.

Michael Spada is director of IEEE Product Launch and Engagement Strategy.

The next standard of handheld gaming continues with the Acer Predator Atlas 8, the striking 8-inch Windows handheld featuring the most powerful chips I've seen for handheld gaming on the go: the Intel Arc G3 Extreme. What really sets this big beauty apart from its rivals, though? It offers a lot for less than you'd think, and I'd be happy to ditch a gaming PC to play on this all day long.

Having seen the Predator Atlas 8's potential back at Computex 2026, I was delighted to see it had met my expectations and gone further, from playing Star Wars: Galactic Racer on the couch to delving deeper into Gears of War: E-Day while travelling with frame rates pushing to 90 frames per second (FPS) at medium to high settings — thanks to Intel's XeSS graphics upscaling and frame generation tech.

It's a marvel to play, only made better thanks to the sizeable 8-inch 1200p LCD display boasting a 120Hz variable refresh rate and the snappy TMR sticks and Hall Effect triggers. For $1,299 / £1,299? That's still pricey, sure, but not nearly as much as the equally powerful $1,799 MSI Claw 8 EX AI+. It's even the same price as the OLED-focused ROG Xbox Ally X20, but delivers even greater power.

All that said, Acer clearly has to make some sacrifices, and they're evident. That includes the cheap-feeling D-pad and adjustable triggers that sometimes don't register input. And don't expect the magic of Intel's XeSS tech to work on a majority of games (including Halo: Campaign Evolved specifically in the Xbox app, despite it being supported, for some odd reason).

In any case, the Acer Predator Atlas 8 is easily one of the best gaming handhelds you can buy right now. For a deeper dive on what to expect, read on.

8-inch FHD+ (1920 x 1200) LCD touchscreen | 120Hz VRR

8-inch FHD+ (1920 x 1200) LCD touchscreen | 120Hz VRR

1x microSD, 2x Thunderbolt 4, 1x 3.5mm audio jack

1x microSD, 2x Thunderbolt 4, 1x 3.5mm audio jack

The Acer Predator Atlas 8 couldn't have arrived in my hands at a better time. I had taken some time off to take care of a new addition to the family (a dog, if you must know), and that meant having plenty of time to build new routines and, of course, kick back. But that all had to be done away from my gaming PC, and my backlog has been piling up (it's been a phenomenal year of great games, and that's pre-GTA VI!).

Thankfully, the Atlas 8 arrived to clean up that backlog, and it's (mostly) been an absolute treat.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

With a name like "Atlas," it's almost a given that this Windows gaming handheld had to be quite big in size. On paper, that should be counterproductive for a portable gaming handheld, but Acer fine-tuned the Predator Atlas 8 to make it a sizeable machine that's equally comfortable to hold, too.

At 11.7 x 5 x 2.2 inches and weighing 1.79 pounds, this is one of the biggest Windows handhelds ever, and that includes comparing it to the famously big Lenovo Legion Go 2 (11.64 x 5.38 x 1.66 inches, 2.09 pounds). At the very least, it isn't nearly as heavy.

But when it comes to the Asus ROG Xbox Ally X20 (11.8 x 4.8 x 2 inches, 1.67 pounds) or MSI Claw 8 EX AI Plus (11.6 x 5.1 x 1.9 inches, 1.7 pounds), it shows Acer couldn't quite trim as much fat off the Atlas 8's bulky design. Realistically, though, there isn't that much difference, and it's still an ergonomically pleasing handheld once put in hands.

From the contoured grip with anti-slip textures to the large layout that rest easy on your palm, the Predator Atlas 8 is great to hold while play all types of gaming genres, whether than be first-person precision in Halo or fast-paced racing in Forza Horizon 6 or Star Wars: Galactic Racer.

While I'd prefer to have an armrest to lay my elbows on while playing, as it is heavier than, say, a Nintendo Switch 2 (10.7 x 4.5 x 0.5 inches, 1.18 pounds), it's still comfy to use. Now, some may find this too bulky and heavy to handle for longer sessions, but setting up in a comfortable position on a couch can fix that issue.

Another major highlight is the 8-inch FHD+ (1920 x 1200) LCD touchscreen with 120Hz VRR. It's big enough to show off great detail and depth in the games I'd play, which is vital in titles like Star Wars: Galactic Racer and even Gears of War: E-Day, and bright enough so I could still see colorful visuals even in sunny environments. With its nicely color-coded face buttons and sticks with RGB-lit rings, it's a great-looking handheld to bring along.

I also really appreciate the satisfying-feeling TMR (Tunnel Magnetoresistance) joysticks and Hall Effect triggers, which make stick drift virtually nonexistent and make each touch feel precise. While the rear macro buttons don't quite feel as premium as the rest, I'm a fan of their placement, along with their customizability for what you need them to do.

A fantastic, great-feeling layout goes a long way in a gaming handheld, and the Atlas 8 nails the design. There's still a lot to be desired (more on that later), but I was always excited to pick this up to start gaming.

Ever since Intel revealed its gaming handheld-specific Intel Arc G3 Extreme, we've seen just how far this chipset has taken portable gaming. It's an incredible chip with plenty of raw power, brought to new heights with Intel XeSS upscaling and frame generation. The Acer Predator Atlas 8 takes that power and runs with it — and it made games I play look far more playable than I'd initially thought.

As in the MSI Claw 8 EX AI+, the Intel Arc G3 Extreme is a wonder for portable power. That's both for graphics and processing power, mind you. AMD's Ryzen Z2 Extreme may have made huge strides to deliver great handheld performance in the ROG Xbox Ally X, but Intel's G3 Extreme takes performance up a notch by a considerable amount. And this shows in every 3DMark test I threw at it.

Acer Predator Atlas 8 (Intel Arc G3 Extreme)

Asus ROG Xbox Ally X (AMD Ryzen Z2 AI Extreme)

Interestingly, despite having the same chipset, the Predator Atlas 8 still fell short of the Claw 8 EX AI+. But that's due to the 24GB of DDR5X RAM my review unit came with compared to the 32GB of DDR5 RAM the Claw 8 EX AI+ boasts. As you can see, there's not a major difference, but do know you can grab a 32GB Atlas 8 model, and it's still less than MSI's handheld.

In any case, even if you wanted to hook up the Atlas 8 to one of the best monitors to get some work done in desktop mode, you can, thanks to the performance this chip offers. To put its Geekbench numbers into perspective, the Atlas 8 is well beyond something like the Dell XPS 13 (2026), and is actually nearly on par with a MacBook Air M4. Now that's impressive.

But this is made to play games, and it has plenty of power to do so. Even with its raw performance, the Atlas 8 offers great frame rates in games like Cyberpunk 2077 at 1080p with High settings and way more in classic titles, including Shadow of the Tomb Raider. Reminder: this is without Intel XeSS upscaling or frame gen.

Acer Predator Atlas 8 (Intel Arc G3 Extreme 35W)

Asus ROG Xbox Ally X20 (AMD Ryzen Z2 AI Extreme 35W)

MSI Claw 8 EX AI+ (Intel Arc G3 Extreme 35W)

This outclasses what the ROG Xbox Ally X20 (and ROG Xbox Ally X, having the same chip) can offer, and surprisingly even beats the Claw 8 EX AI+ by a few frames. For the price, this is an amazing feat, and well worth the performance alone. That's especially true for older classics, too, as you can get over 80 FPS in the likes of Shadow of the Tomb Raider.

Of course, it wouldn't be enjoyable to play the latest titles at those measly frame rates. But even at Medium settings in Black Myth: Wukong, you can get a solid 47 FPS, and that's at 1200p resolution. With a bit of tinkering in the settings (like a resolution drop or some low settings), you can get this running at 60 FPS without frame gen needed.

Now, once I started bringing Intel XeSS upscaling into the fold, that's when you can really see the Atlas 8 work its magic. Think Cyberpunk 2077 at 1200p with frame rates reaching past 90 FPS, and that's with High settings and ray tracing turned on. Similarly, Star Wars: Galactic Racer at 1200p with Medium quality and Balanced resolution scaling was hitting over 70 FPS, which is needed for that type of fast-paced gameplay.

Even Gears of War: E-Day performed brilliantly, whether I wanted a solid 60 FPS with Quality upscaling or closer to 90 FPS and up for faster performance. As you can tell, there's a lot the Intel Arc G3 Extreme can handle, especially with XeSS tech to back it up (where it's supported). If you're after a gaming powerhouse for the road, the Acer Predator Atlas 8 is up to the challenge.

Despite the power the Predator Atlas 8 boasts, this Windows handheld has the battery life that can see you through gaming sessions that last hours — when you need it to.

Through the PredatorSense menu on the Atlas 8, Acer made it easy to switch between power wattage modes, including Quiet (25W), Balanced (30W) and Turbo (35W). But you can also manually change power from 10W all the way up to 40W (and up to 65W for short bursts of power, even though this isn't recommended by the system).

All of this to say you can have the Atlas 8 utilize a lot of power to push performance further, or have it sip on battery for less demanding games. The end result is long-lasting battery life, reaching nearly 4 hours in testing.

3DMark gaming battery life test result (hh:mm)

This isn't quite as long as the MSI Claw 8 EX AI+, but it's nearly a full hour longer than what the ROG Xbox Ally X offers. It's nice to see handhelds now going past the 3-hour mark, as I could now get a proper gaming session in without needing to be tethered to a charger.

During real-world gameplay, I saw the Atlas 8 last 1 hour and 35 minutes while playing Gears of War: E-Day, and 1 hour and 41 minutes in Cyberpunk 2077, both at 35W. Switching to 25W while still getting good performance, Star Wars: Galactic Racer lasted 2 hours and 24 minutes. Not bad for those types of demanding titles! But when it comes to less-demanding games like Hades 2 or Marvel Cosmic Invasion, with only 10-15W, this only went down to 85% in an hour. That's a long time to game!

Usually, I'd imagine powerful performance results in incredibly short battery life. But more and more, we're seeing this isn't the case, and the Predator Atlas 8 is a fine example of this.

As much as I've enjoyed playing on the Acer Predator Atlas 8 any chance I got, it's still held back by a few sacrifices being made, which I imagine were done to keep the price down. That, and there are still some Windows 11 hiccups here and there (although, that's hardly surprising).

While the Acer Predator Atlas 8 feels comfy in the hand thanks to its ergonomic grips, anti-slip texture and satisfying heft, it's still quite a chunky piece of tech. Not everyone will appreciate holding nearly 1.8 pounds for hours on end, especially when its rivals are lighter.

This wasn't a major problem for me, especially when I had my elbows resting on the armrests of my office chair or the side of the couch. That said, the aches were starting to creep in while traveling. It's a big handheld to deliver a large 8-inch display and comfy grips, and I wouldn't expect otherwise from a device named "Atlas." Just know what you're signing up for. At the very least, you can drop to the Predator Atlas 7 for a smaller 7-inch design.

Bringing TMR joysticks for precise, good-feeling controls that are stick drift-resistant, along with Hall Effect analog triggers for pleasing responsiveness, is hugely welcome, but the D-pad seems to have been thrown in without much thought.

There's no tactile feel or satisfying actuation feedback for each direction here, just what feels like one big mushy button. For the majority of games, this isn't a huge deal, as you'll be using the analog sticks anyway. But for classic titles, fighting games, Metroidvanias and more, having a great D-pad makes a world of difference. I know this, as while playing Guile in Street Fighter 6, buttons just couldn't reliably register a charging-type "Sonic Boom." With how smooth the D-pad feels, I suppose it did make the input for Ryu's "Hadoken" somewhat easier, but never consistent.

It's also worth noting that the Predator Atlas 8 comes with adjustable trigger modes, which let you change the L2 and R2 triggers from full-travel analog press to shorter travel for faster inputs. This is a great addition, but I noticed that switching to a shorter trigger meant some actions didn't register (such as shooting a weapon). This could be a minor issue with my unit, but also something to keep aware of. Otherwise, switching back to full travel didn't make a huge difference anyway.

Microsoft's Xbox Mode has made a world of difference on Windows handhelds to deliver more of a console-like experience. But it still has some issues to iron out.

While I love bringing up the Xbox overlay to quickly switch gaming clients, check out my library of games, change settings and also see performance (that includes FPS), sometimes the overlay simply wouldn't come up unless I pressed the menu button a few times, or never at all until I switched apps. The same thing would happen when pressing the power button to put it to sleep — sometimes it powered down immediately, sometimes it didn't.

I also appreciate being able to switch to desktop mode to, essentially, use this like a proper PC. But again, nuisances like the keyboard not coming up when trying to find a game on Steam or the Xbox app being open but not showing up on screen make it all frustrating. Windows 11 on handhelds still isn't as clean to use as, say, SteamOS, but it's far from what it was.

Also, like the MSI Claw 8 EX AI+, Intel's XeSS 3 support in games is still limited. While games like Star Wars: Galactic Racer, Assassin’s Creed Black Flag Resynced and Forza Horizon 6 support this for Multi-Frame Generation (MFG), many of the biggest titles still don't. In fact, Halo: Campaign Evolved does support Intel XeSS 3, but it's "not available for Microsoft Store games," strangely. So, that means I would have to buy this on Steam to get access instead. That's annoying.

The Intel Arc G3 Extreme chip is still plenty powerful, and more games will be supported in the future, but there are some limits to know about.

The Acer Predator Atlas 8 has been hard for me to put down, and that should say plenty about how much I've enjoyed playing all the latest PC titles on this mighty machine. From the outstanding performance the Intel Arc G3 Extreme chip delivers in even demanding games to the big, bright 8-inch display to get stuck into, the Atlas 8 is a fantastic gaming handheld that I've been happy to use virtually anywhere instead of my gaming PC.

What sets it apart from its rivals? It's price-to-performance ratio. It's more affordable than the MSI Claw 8 EX AI+ while delivering the same performance, and it's the same price as the ROG Xbox Ally X20 while being more powerful. But design-wise, Acer's handheld doesn't quite match all the premium trimmings of its competition.

In any case, that doesn't take away from the Acer Predator Atlas 8 being the best gaming handheld I've tested, so if you're looking for the ultimate gaming experience on the move, this will certainly fit the bill.
